name: french-basics

description.en: 120 basic French words and phrases for beginners: the numbers 0–20, the tens and 100, the days of the week, the months, eight colours, family members, greetings and polite phrases, everyday nouns, six adjectives and 16 verbs. The front shows the French word, nouns with their article (le livre, la maison; before a vowel or mute h, l' with the gender added: l'eau (f.)); the back gives its English and Swedish meaning, or the digits for a number, and for days and months a note on their gender. Words and genders from Wikidata's lexemes and the US Foreign Service Institute's French Basic Course (public domain), English and Swedish meanings from Wikidata where it has them and otherwise the authors' own, all checked against French, English and Swedish Wiktionary, the Lexique 3 database and Folkets lexikon.
description.sv: 120 grundläggande franska ord och fraser för nybörjare: talen 0–20, tiotalen och 100, veckodagarna, månaderna, åtta färger, familjemedlemmar, hälsningar och artighetsfraser, vardagliga substantiv, sex adjektiv och 16 verb. Framsidan visar det franska ordet, substantiv med sin artikel (le livre, la maison; före vokal eller stumt h skrivs l' och genus anges: l'eau (f.)); baksidan ger betydelsen på engelska och svenska, eller siffrorna för ett tal, och för veckodagar och månader en anteckning om genus. Ord och genus från Wikidatas lexem och amerikanska Foreign Service Institutes French Basic Course (fri från upphovsrätt), engelska och svenska betydelser från Wikidata där sådana finns och annars författarnas egna, alla kontrollerade mot franska, engelska och svenska Wiktionary, databasen Lexique 3 och Folkets lexikon.

method: Who did the work. Anton Wiklund compiled this deck with the help of AI agents (Claude, by Anthropic), which did the research, drafting and cross-checking at his direction. The cards were checked by machine (live Wikidata and the app's SHACL and DCAT-AP validators) and in independent review rounds by further Claude agents, each logged under Quality control with its findings and how they were resolved. Anton Wiklund reviews every deck in full before it is released.

Word list. A candidate list of 120 words and phrases for a first French course was drawn up by hand from the brief's categories (numbers 0–20, the tens and 100; days; months; colours; family; greetings and polite phrases; everyday nouns; adjectives; verbs), choosing the most basic word for each concept, the same as the first authored Spanish deck where the languages allow. No frequency list or textbook word list was copied; Lexique 3's frequency columns were not consulted.

Wikidata lexemes. SPARQL query 1 fetched every French lexeme (language Q150) whose lemma is a candidate, with its category, gender (P5185), senses, English and French glosses and sense items (P5137). Six candidates were not found: quatre-vingts and five phrases. The lexeme search (API calls 2) found quatre-vingt (L10500, lemma without s) but no lexeme for au revoir, à bientôt, s'il vous plaît, je vous en prie, excusez-moi or de rien (je vous en prie was searched in review round 3, see call 2; it too returns no lexeme). So the five phrases on the cards without a lexeme are au revoir, à bientôt, s'il vous plaît, je vous en prie and excusez-moi; de rien, a sixth phrase without one, is not a card. The full JSON of the lexeme chosen for each word (the numeral lexeme for numbers, the noun lexeme for nouns, the adjective lexeme for colours and adjectives, and so on) was fetched with API calls 3, and the English and Swedish lexemes named by the senses' translation statements (P5972) with API calls 4.

Wikidata items. The items linked from the chosen senses (P5137), plus four items found with the item search (API calls 6: good evening Q19279366, goodbye Q2506912, hello Q12068060, thank you Q19279214), were fetched with API calls 5 (labels and aliases in fr, en, sv and mul). They gave the English and Swedish names of days, months, colours, family members, greetings and everyday things and the digit labels of the numbers. Where a sense has several items, the one for the card's meaning was used (eau: Q283 water; porte: sense S3, Q36794 door, not S1, Q53060 gate).

Phrases from the FSI course. For the five phrases with no Wikidata lexeme, the Internet Archive was searched for public-domain Foreign Service Institute French courses (call 8) and the OCR text of the French Basic Course (Revised), volumes 1 and 2, was downloaded (call 9). Au revoir, à bientôt, excusez-moi (Unit 1 dialogue), s'il vous plaît (Unit 1, classroom expressions, and a Unit 5 drill) and je vous en prie (Unit 2 dialogue, the reply to Merci beaucoup, glossed "You're welcome") were found with grep (call 10) and read in context with the English column. De rien does not occur as a phrase in either volume (only in sentences such as Je n'ai besoin de rien), nor in the FSI Metropolitan French FAST course, whose text was also searched (call 11). The deck's reply to merci is je vous en prie, the reply the public-domain course gives; de rien, the more casual reply with the same meaning, is named in its note rather than given a card of its own, since its back would be the same (the authors' knowledge of usage, confirmed by French Wiktionary). FSI's OCR text has no accents; the accented spellings come from French Wiktionary and Lexique.

Writing the cards. The front is the French word as in the lexeme's lemma (or FSI's phrase), lower case. Nouns are preceded by the definite article that shows their gender (le livre, la maison). Convention for elided articles: before a vowel or mute h the article is written l' and the gender is added in brackets, m. or f. (l'eau (f.), l'école (f.), l'homme (m.), l'ami (m.)); the apostrophe is the straight ASCII apostrophe, as in s'il vous plaît. Days and months are given without an article, as usually written, with their gender in a note. Colours and adjectives are given in the masculine singular with the feminine in a note; verbs in the infinitive. The back is our own short English and Swedish rendering of the main sense: for nouns the bare noun, for verbs the infinitive (English "to …", Swedish "att …"), for numbers the digits (tagged zxx, as digits are in no language). English and Swedish follow the Wikidata labels where an item exists and has them; otherwise they are the usual equivalents, chosen by the authors and checked in English Wiktionary, Folkets lexikon and Swedish Wiktionary (step 8). Where a French word has two everyday English or Swedish equivalents both are given (fille: daughter, girl; grand: big, tall; aller: gå, åka; aimer: love, like). Rule for text not given by a content source: English and Swedish equivalents and the facts behind the notes come from the authors' own knowledge of the languages, are worded by the authors and are only confirmed in the verification sources; such single words and short facts of usage count as the authors' own content. Where a back coincides with a verification source's gloss, the enwiktionary source record says so. Swedish backs are chosen in the register of the French: s'il vous plaît, which is polite, is "vänligen" (Folkets: särskilt i artighetsuttryck), not the colloquial "snälla" (Swedish Wiktionary: vardagligt) (review round 1).

Notes. A short note was added where it helps a beginner and is confirmed by a source: the gender of each day and month (shown for days with the indefinite article, un lundi, since le lundi means on Mondays), the feminine of each colour and adjective (nouvel and vieil before a masculine singular noun beginning with a vowel or mute h, confirmed by the French and English Wiktionary pages nouvel and vieil), un as the indefinite article, neuf also meaning new (with a front note "number" on neuf and un, and "colour" on orange), soixante-dix, quatre-vingts and quatre-vingt-dix with the Belgian and Swiss septante and nonante, quatre-vingt without s before another number, the pronunciation of fils, femme also meaning wife, homme also a human being, l'amie, la livre (pound), bonjour by day and bonsoir in the evening, salut and the tu/vous forms s'il te plaît and excuse-moi, de rien, Swedish requests ending with tack and snälla being colloquial, and the Swedish gå/åka distinction. Notes are our own wording.

Cross-checking. Every French word and phrase was looked up in French Wiktionary (calls 13): spelling, part of speech, the gender mark on the head line against the article on the card, and the first relevant definition (quoted in each card's evidence). Every word was also looked up in Lexique 3.83 (call 16) for spelling, category and gender. Every English meaning was checked against the French section of English Wiktionary (calls 14). Every Swedish word was checked in Folkets lexikon (call 17), English → Swedish, or Swedish → English when the first direction had no match, and, where a page exists, in the French entry of Swedish Wiktionary (calls 15). A Python script built the evidence lines from the responses saved during authoring, so each quote is what the source returned, with wiki markup and footnote references removed (the parsing logic is given with the calls); quotations longer than 160 characters are cut and marked with "…". The raw responses and scripts were working files and are not published.

Dictionaries not used. The brief suggested the Dictionnaire de l'Académie française and Larousse for checking the French. Their terms were read first: the Académie's conditions (https://www.dictionnaire-academie.fr/CGU) forbid "d’utiliser tout système automatisé ou logiciel pour aspirer ou extraire des données du Site", and Larousse's (https://www.larousse.fr/infos/cgu) state that it "s’oppose à toutes opérations de moissonnage et de fouille de textes et de données", including automated collection. Before reading them, the authoring agent had made a few test requests to find out how the sites work (Académie: the page https://www.dictionnaire-academie.fr/search?term=maison, its script /js/scriptAF.js, two POST requests to /search with term=maison, and the entry https://www.dictionnaire-academie.fr/article/A9M0242; Larousse: https://www.larousse.fr/dictionnaires/francais/maison); their content was not used for any card, and neither dictionary was consulted further. French Wiktionary and Lexique 3, whose licences allow automated use, took their place.

Machine checks. The dossier's Wikidata checks (the French, English and Swedish label or alias of each linked item that matches the card's text, and the mul digit label of each number) are re-run against live Wikidata by the builder on every build. Wikidata lexemes cannot be checked by the builder (it checks items only); the lexeme facts in the evidence were read from the API responses of 4 October 2026. The built deck was validated with the app's SHACL and DCAT-AP validators (scripts/validate_sources.ts).

Excluded: de rien as a card of its own (it means the same as je vous en prie, the reply in the public-domain FSI course, and is named in that card's note), words with two equally common meanings that a single card cannot separate (le temps: time or weather; la glace: ice or mirror; la pièce: room or coin), brown and purple (marron or brun; violet or mauve), words whose everyday form differs between France, Belgium, Switzerland and Canada beyond the tens noted on the cards (déjeuner, dîner, souper), the formal/informal pairs tu and vous (which need grammar, not a flashcard), the year (an and année, two words for one concept), and connaître/savoir (both to know).
selection: 120 cards: the cardinal numbers 0–20, the tens 30–90 and 100 (29); the seven days of the week; the twelve months; eight colours (red, blue, green, yellow, black, white, grey, orange); eight family members (mother, father, brother, sister, son, daughter, grandfather, grandmother); twelve greetings and polite phrases (bonjour, bonsoir, bonne nuit, salut, au revoir, à bientôt, merci, s'il vous plaît, je vous en prie, excusez-moi, oui, non); 22 everyday nouns (house, water, bread, milk, apple, book, table, chair, door, window, dog, cat, town, street, school, man, woman, friend, hand, day, night, week); six common adjectives (grand, petit, bon, mauvais, nouveau, vieux); and 16 common verbs in the infinitive (être, avoir, aller, faire, venir, parler, manger, boire, aimer, vouloir, pouvoir, voir, lire, écrire, dormir, travailler). The list was chosen by the deck's authors for a first course, not copied from any frequency list or textbook. Every word has a Wikidata lexeme except the five phrases noted in the method, which come from the public-domain FSI course. Left out: de rien as a card of its own (same meaning as je vous en prie, which the FSI course gives as the reply to merci; it is named in that card's note), words with two equally common meanings (temps, glace, pièce), brown and purple (several competing words), words for meals whose meaning differs between France, Belgium, Switzerland and Canada, tu/vous, the pair an/année, and connaître/savoir. Nouns are given with the definite article; before a vowel or mute h the elided l' is followed by the gender, (m.) or (f.). Colours and adjectives are given in the masculine singular, with the feminine in a note. Days and months are given without an article and in lower case, as French writes them; their gender is in a note on every day and month card. Numbers are the standard forms of France (soixante-dix, quatre-vingts, quatre-vingt-dix), with the Belgian and Swiss septante and nonante in notes.

findings.issue: The brief named the Dictionnaire de l'Académie française and Larousse for checking the French, but both sites' terms forbid automated extraction (the Académie's CGU section 5; Larousse's opposition to text and data mining under article L. 122-5-3 of the French intellectual property code).
